item.title: PulseFlow: Turning a Webcam into a Real-Time Human-Sensing Experience
item.description:

This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.

PulseFlow: Turning a Webcam into a Real-Time Human-Sensing Experience

Your body, in real time.

What if exploring your body's physiological signals didn't require a smartwatch, fitness tracker, or specialized hardware?

What if all you needed was a webcam?

That question inspired me to build PulseFlow, a Windows desktop application powered by the Presage SmartSpectra SDK that turns ordinary camera input into a real-time human-sensing experience.

PulseFlow combines contactless heart rate and breathing rate estimation with live charts, guided breathing sessions, and meaningful session summaries.

I wanted to explore how complex physiological sensing technology could become a simple, approachable, and privacy-conscious desktop experience.

What I Built

I built PulseFlow, a desktop application developed with Electron, Node.js, TypeScript, and Presage SmartSpectra.

The application uses a standard webcam to estimate physiological signals and presents them through a minimal interface designed for clarity and ease of use.

Rather than building only a technical monitoring dashboard, I wanted to create an experience that people could interact with.

PulseFlow has three main components:

1. Real-Time Physiological Monitoring

PulseFlow requests two physiological measurements from SmartSpectra:

- Heart Rate: Estimated pulse in beats per minute (BPM).

- Breathing Rate: Estimated respiratory frequency in breaths per minute (br/min).

The application displays accepted readings through live numerical indicators and time-series charts.

Users can also see camera status, signal availability, and feedback when capture conditions need improvement.

2. Guided Breathing

I wanted users to do more than simply observe their measurements.

PulseFlow includes a guided breathing experience with:

- Configurable inhalation and exhalation durations.

- A minimal animated breathing indicator.

- Start, pause, resume, and end controls.

- A synchronized session timer.

- Physiological measurement collection during the exercise.

The breathing animation is driven by the exercise timer, not by artificially generated physiological measurements.

3. Session Summaries

At the end of a session, PulseFlow provides a summary containing:

- Total session duration.

- Average observed heart rate.

- Average observed breathing rate.

- Number of valid samples for each signal.

- Session completion status.

These statistics are calculated from accepted SmartSpectra measurements collected during the exercise.

Design Philosophy

PulseFlow follows a minimalist, monochromatic design direction influenced by modern developer tools and the Geist design language.

The interface emphasizes readable physiological metrics, subtle borders, restrained animations, real-time charts, and contextual notifications.

My goal was to make complex sensing technology feel understandable without overwhelming the user.

Real Measurements, Not Simulations

An important requirement I set for myself was that PulseFlow should not fabricate physiological readings.

These values came from an actual demonstration rather than hardcoded data.

When valid measurements are unavailable, the application displays an appropriate waiting state instead of inventing readings.

Demo

I recorded a demonstration showing PulseFlow running with a real webcam and the Presage SmartSpectra SDK.

The video showcases live physiological monitoring, the guided breathing experience, and a completed session summary.

Watch the full demonstration on YouTube

For privacy, the public recording uses anonymized camera imagery while preserving the live physiological measurements displayed by the application.

Code

The complete source code is publicly available on GitHub:

The repository includes the Electron application, native SmartSpectra integration, measurement-processing logic, guided breathing functionality, tests, screenshots, and setup instructions.

Technology Stack

Running PulseFlow Locally

Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/Ezequie1Sc/PulseFlow.git

cd PulseFlow

Install dependencies:

npm ci

Create a local environment file.

On Windows PowerShell:

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Configure your Presage SmartSpectra API key in .env:

SMARTSPECTRA_API_KEY=your_presage_api_key

Start the desktop application:

npm run dev

A compatible webcam, camera permissions, and a valid API key are required.

The repository's README contains additional information about installation, application architecture, privacy, and troubleshooting.

How It Responds to Human Signals

The Presage SmartSpectra SDK is the foundation of PulseFlow.

The application uses live camera-based physiological estimates rather than simulated datasets.

1. Camera-Based Signal Acquisition

After the user explicitly consents to monitoring, PulseFlow initializes the SmartSpectra Node.js SDK and connects to a selected webcam.

The application requests these metrics:

MetricType.PULSE_RATE,

PulseFlow checks incoming measurements using its validation and filtering logic.

If SmartSpectra cannot provide a suitable signal, the interface communicates that state rather than presenting fabricated numbers.

item.title: Your agent's rule pack is only as good as its install script
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

This is the adapted syndication of a longer review first published on AI Stack Lab: RulePort Review: I Ran Its Installer Six Ways. The blogger version has the full command-by-command transcript.

Your agent's rule pack is only as good as its install script

Every "rule pack" sold to people running two or more coding agents makes the same three promises: one source of truth, one installer, and a drift check that tells you when the files on disk no longer match what you bought. The first promise is an authoring choice. The second and third are code, and code can be tested.

So I tested them. I unzipped RulePort ($1 on Gumroad, 58 files, 12 rules) into an empty directory, copied it to a scratch tree, and ran its installer six ways: dry-run, real, twice to check idempotency, over hand-written files, on a machine with no agents at all, and against deliberate drift. Then I hashed the trees before and after each run so "unchanged" meant a matching sha256, not a hopeful reading of the console.

Four claims held. Two leaked. Here is what that looked like.

The parts that held

The compiler is byte-stable. python3 tools/ruleport.py compile printed compiled 12 rules -> 39 files. I hashed the shipped compiled/ tree, compiled, hashed again, compiled a third time, hashed again. Zero files changed in either direction. This sounds like a low bar and it is not: a compiler that reorders its own output every run makes every commit dirty and turns the drift check into noise. This one is deterministic.

--dry-run actually writes nothing. Not "writes then tells you" — I hashed the target directory before and after and it was empty.

Install is idempotent. First run: 39 files. Second run, same command: every file reported unchanged, and the sha256 map of the whole tree was identical. No duplication, no second marker comment, no churn.

It refuses to eat your own files. I planted a hand-written CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md with no RulePort marker and ran the full install. Both were skipped and left byte-identical. --force replaced them deliberately, as documented. That default matters more than the feature list: an installer that silently overwrites a CLAUDE.md you wrote is worse than no installer at all.

The fallback fires. On a fresh HOME with agent binaries stripped out of PATH, install.sh printed no runtimes detected and wrote exactly one file: ./AGENTS.md. The README's claim about the universal fallback is true on a machine with nothing installed.

diff means what an exit code should mean — mostly. Fresh install: in sync — installed files match the compiled pack, exit 0. Append one line to a single .mdc rule and re-run: exit 1, with a real unified diff naming the file. Bad arguments exit 2 with usage. I will take a tool that shouts over one that guesses.

The two leaks

Leak one: diff can report "in sync" over zero files. Run it in a directory where nothing was ever installed and it prints one not installed … — skipped line per runtime, then in sync — installed files match the compiled pack and exit 0. Four runtimes skipped, zero files compared, green tick.

If you follow the README and wire that exit code into CI as your drift gate, a machine where the install never happened passes. You have to read the comparing N file(s) lines, or assert on a file count you expect, instead of trusting the number.

I want to be fair about this: a drift check with nothing to compare arguably is in sync with an empty installed set. But that is not the sentence anyone reads at 2am when the CI is green and the agent is still following last month's rules. A gate that can pass by comparing nothing is exactly the false confidence this class of tool exists to remove.

Leak two: "claude detected" means a claude binary is on PATH. Detection is [ -d "$HOME/.claude" ] || command -v claude. On my box that fired and the installer wrote 14 files into ~/.claude — globally, from a project directory, without asking. The README's table says Claude Code lands in ~/.claude/ (global) or .claude/ (per project), but bash install.sh only ever does the global one. To get a project-local .claude/ you must call python3 tools/ruleport.py install --agent claude --target <dir> directly. I confirmed both by doing both.

Neither leak is dishonest — the behaviour is documented loosely enough to be defensible. But "global by default" plus "green drift check that compared nothing" is a pair of surprises worth knowing before you buy, so they belong in the review, not in a footnote.

What is in the box, counted

- 58 files, 174,768 bytes unpacked, 103,003 bytes as the zip.

- 12 canonical rule files — the only place you edit.

- 39 compiled outputs: 12 Cursor .mdc, 14 Claude Code files (12 skills + CLAUDE.md + a /ruleport-status command), 12 Windsurf, 1 AGENTS.md (24,336 bytes, all 12 rules).

- tools/ruleport.py: 457 lines, imports only argparse, difflib, pathlib, shutil, sys. Standard library, so there is no dependency graph to audit and no network call at compile time.

- install.sh: 111 lines. Plus docs/customization.md and docs/update-policy.md.

The 12 rules are deliberately boring: verify before done, test first, error handling, types and docstrings, security baseline, self code review, database safety, API design, dependency hygiene, git hygiene, frontend accessibility, docs updates. They are the ones that stop the classic agent failure — the confident "done" over untested code, the swallowed exception, the dependency added for a problem the standard library already solved.

Who should skip it

- You run exactly one agent. A compiler that emits four formats is pure overhead for one consumer. Hand-write your rules.

- Your team already maintains a conventions tree that agents read. You have a source of truth; a second one is a liability.

- You need a drift gate you can trust blind. Because of leak one, you must assert on the compared-file count, not the exit code alone.

- You want rules generated from source. This ships opinionated prose, not a linter and not a static analyser.…

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-22 05:42 UTC

Original link: https://dev.to/the_movie_9b1357e8c99cfaa/your-agents-rule-pack-is-only-as-good-as-its-install-script-3l3o

item.title: Por que o COMP-3 do COBOL ainda derruba integrações com Pix e ISO 20022 (e uma ferramenta open-source)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Quem trabalha com engenharia de backend em bancos, adquirentes ou fintechs no Brasil conhece bem um contraste curioso: na ponta do cliente, o sistema liquida transações em segundos via Pix e troca mensagens estruturadas em XML/JSON no padrão ISO 20022; no núcleo contábil, porém, uma parcela enorme das instituições ainda processa saldos e lotes em mainframes COBOL.

O ponto de fratura mais silencioso nessa ponte não costuma ser a latência da API, e sim a tradução de dados binários — em especial o formato COMP-3 (Packed Decimal).

O que é o COMP-3 na prática?

Em vez de armazenar dígitos em ASCII/UTF-8 (1 byte por dígito) ou usar ponto flutuante IEEE 754 (que introduz erros de arredondamento inaceitáveis em centavos), o COBOL armazena dois dígitos decimais por byte — um em cada nibble (4 bits) — e reserva o último nibble do último byte para o sinal:

- 0xC: positivo

- 0xD: negativo

- 0xF: sem sinal (unsigned)

Por exemplo, o valor +12345.67 definido como PIC S9(5)V99 COMP-3 ocupa exatamente 4 bytes em disco ou na fila de mensageria: 12 34 56 7C (7 dígitos + 1 nibble de sinal).

Três bugs comuns em integrações Pix / ISO 20022

-

Conversão para float ou double: qualquer passagem intermediária por ponto flutuante binário pode corromper frações de centavo na reconciliação de fim de dia. Use sempre precisão fixa (BigDecimal, Decimal, ou inteiros em centavos).

-

Ponto decimal implícito (V): o V no PIC S9(5)V99 não ocupa espaço em byte. Se o parser errar a escala implícita, R$ 100,00 viram R$ 10.000,00 ou R$ 1,00.

-

Interpretação incorreta do nibble de sinal: tratar 0xD como positivo ou falhar ao ler 0xF gera lançamentos invertidos que só aparecem no batimento contábil.

Ferramenta open-source para depurar direto no navegador

Na Digbijoy Labs construímos um inspetor open-source que roda 100% no navegador (sem backend e sem envio de dados) para codificar, decodificar e visualizar payloads COMP-3 nibble a nibble:

- Inspetor online (zero instalação): https://digbijoylabs.github.io/iron-silicon-bridge/

- Código-fonte no GitHub: https://github.com/digbijoylabs/iron-silicon-bridge

- Referência técnica aberta (CERN Zenodo DOI): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24243905

- Livro técnico (The Iron–Silicon Bridge): https://digbijoylabs.com/books/the-iron-silicon-bridge/

Para quem já trabalhou com modernização de legado ou integração de core bancário com Pix: qual foi o bug mais traiçoeiro de encoding ou paridade de dados que vocês enfrentaram?

item.title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to Standardize Parts to Lower Costs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

- Toyota, Nissan, and Honda will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by Automotive News.

- The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses.

- Discussions are starting with Japan’s domestic suppliers, though international suppliers will be looped in soon.

Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.

In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.

The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report.

The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into new innovations.

“We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato said. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.”

Source: Hacker News | Published: 2026-11-22 04:04 UTC

item.title: Together.ai: Prompt Leakage for Requests
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

We are notifying customers about a security incident involving a subset of prompts submitted to Together AI’s serverless inference service in June and July 2026. An unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples after a credential for a private repository was exposed in a public code repository.

We apologize for this incident. We are reviewing the affected data to determine what information was exposed and which customers require direct notification.

What happened

As part of routine software testing, we collected prompt samples authorized for that use and stored them in a private Hugging Face repository. The samples came from requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models, primarily on June 24, July 4, July 8, and July 14, 2026.

During development of our public GitHub repository, xorl, an AI coding agent committed a credential that provided access to the private Hugging Face repository. Our automated scanning detected the exposed credential, and we reverted the commit.

During the exposure window, an unauthorized party obtained the credential and used it to download the stored prompt samples. The party subsequently searched those samples for credentials to other services and tested whether those credentials were valid. Five of the credentials tested were canary credentials associated with a Dragos security experiment.

We have no reason to believe the unauthorized party has leaked this data further and understand that it has now been deleted.

Investigation and scope

We have worked with an external forensic investigation firm and law enforcement to investigate the incident.

Based on our review, we have not identified evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this incident. Our review of the affected prompt contents is ongoing to determine whether sensitive personal information or other customer data was exposed. We will contact affected customers directly as needed with the findings relevant to them.

Changes we have made

Following the incident, we strengthened controls around development workflows, credentials, and customer data. These changes include:

- Using scoped or short-lived credentials, and keyless access where supported, to reduce the potential impact of credential exposure.

- Checking all pull requests for credentials.

- Making zero data retention (ZDR) the default setting for new accounts.

- Updating our development processes governing the use of AI coding agents.

What customers can do

Customers handling sensitive prompt data should enable ZDR in their account settings.

If you have questions about this incident or its potential impact on your organization, contact security@together.ai.

Vipul Ved Prakash

CEO and Co-founder, Together AI

Source: Hacker News | Published: 2026-11-22 03:07 UTC

item.title: Attention Pixel 9 and 10 owners: is it actually worth upgrading to the Pixel 11?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Attention Pixel 9 and 10 owners: is it actually worth upgrading to the Pixel 11?

Pixel 10 owners can skip this one. Pixel 9 owners have a real decision to make.

Google's new Pixel 11 went on sale in August 2026, but new doesn't always mean better. It uses the same 6.3-inch display and 5x telephoto camera as the previous year's model; has the same 12GB of RAM; and its battery is just 15mAh bigger. You'll enjoy double the storage space, but it also costs $899, which is $100 more than the launch price of the Pixel 10.

If the question is whether it's worth upgrading from the 10 to the 11, the answer is no. Keep the phone you've got. If you're a Pixel 9 owner, the advantages are more pronounced. Jumping two generations gets you a telephoto lens, better battery life and an additional two years of software updates, making the upgrade a worthy consideration.

What's new compared to the Pixel 10

With the Pixel 11, you get a Tensor G6 chip, which replaces last year's Tensor G5. Google claims the G6 gives users 25 percent improvements in web browsing speed, alongside 15 percent improvements in app launches. The 48MP main camera gets a larger sensor that's reportedly 56 percent more sensitive to light, and Super Zoom reaches 30x instead of 20x. Wireless charging has increased from 15W to 25W, and the phone now comes with 256GB rather than 128GB.

While 30x zoom sounds impressive, our hands-on testing found that these zoom shots looked fine on the phone's screen but lost a lot of detail once we opened them on a laptop. The phone itself was quick and fluid, though admittedly nothing we threw at it pushed it very hard.

On its comparison page with the Pixel 10, Google lists two camera features as exclusive to the Pixel 11: Magic Capture and Camera Looks. Magic Capture records a short clip and pulls out the best frames as stills, while Camera Looks lets you set and tweak a default filter. However, Android Central's Harish Jonnalagadda argues that most of this year's software additions will reach older Pixels through Google's regular updates anyway. Once you take those away (or, rather, add them to the Pixel 10), you may be essentially paying for a faster chip, double the base memory and quicker wireless charging. That's hard to justify at $899, especially if you bought the Pixel 10 in 2025.

It's a different story for Pixel 9 owners

The Pixel 9 has two rear cameras, a 50MP main and a 48MP ultrawide, and tops out at 8x Super Res Zoom. To that, the Pixel 11 adds a 10.8MP telephoto camera with a 5x optical zoom and optical image stabilization. That's more optical reach than the $799 iPhone 17, which has no telephoto at all, or the $899 Galaxy S26, whose 10MP telephoto stops at 3x. When we reviewed the Pixel 11, that telephoto was its main advantage over phones at the same price. It's not a Pro camera, though. The Pixel 11 Pro's telephoto uses a 48MP, 1/1.95-inch sensor, while the base model makes do with a 1/3.2-inch sensor.

In terms of its battery, the Pixel 9 has a 4,700mAh that Google rates for more than 24 hours, while the Pixel 11's 4,985mAh cell is rated for more than 30 hours. In our testing, the Pixel 11 lasted from 8AM on a Saturday to 7PM on Sunday on a single charge. You'll also get Pixelsnap magnets built in with the 11, so magnetic Qi2 chargers and mounts attach without a case, which can't be done with the Pixel 9. The 11's screen is also brighter, peaking at 3,000 nits against the Pixel 9's 2,700.

Google Pixel software support

Google promises seven years of OS and security updates from the date each Pixel first went on sale in the United States. That puts the end of software updates for the Pixel 9 at August 2031, the Pixel 10 at August 2032 and the Pixel 11 at August 2033, so none of these models are anywhere near being left behind yet. If you're struggling with your Pixel 9's battery life, something which has admittedly led me to prematurely upgrade my phone in the past, a genuine replacement will set you back about $50 at iFixit. Google can also provide price quotes for its mail-in repair service through an online estimator.

In our opinion, Pixel 10 owners should definitely consider hanging on until at least the Pixel 12 because, as we said earlier, you're not getting that much more for your money. The telephoto lens is the real draw for Pixel 9 owners who could benefit from having better zoom — a feature that no software update can add. But if your Pixel 9 still gets you through the day and you rarely venture beyond 2x zoom, there's no pressing reason to fork out $899 right now.

item.title: Samsung vs. LG OLED TVs: What's the difference between them?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Samsung vs. LG OLED TVs: What's the difference between them?

It's not simple to say that one is better than the other.

LG and Samsung continue to dominate the OLED TV market. LG entered the field in 2010 with its humble 15-inch 15EL9500 during the technology's infancy, laying the groundwork for its first 55-inch television in 2012. Throughout the years, LG has slowly built a major foothold in the space with its series of OLED displays. Their crisp colors gives it a unique pop you seldom find in other OLED televisions, even those with more impressive spec sheets.

And you won't find more impressive spec sheets than Samsung OLEDs. Since its return to the OLED TV market in 2022, the company has invested heavily in display-panel innovations to carve out its own niche. Samsung's QD-OLEDs are arguably the sharpest-looking OLEDs you'll find in consumer-grade hardware, outperforming LG's panels in color saturation. Based on that, you might think Samsung would be the clear winner for OLED TVs, yet LG's latest OLED innovations make the decision less black-and-white.

Samsung has continued to struggle to provide accurate information about its televisions, obfuscating which panel technologies it uses. LG has faced similar criticism for its major quality concerns with the launch of the G6. Finding the perfect television goes far beyond finding a good panel type. The brand, the television's software and your viewing area should play a key role in your decision.

Samsung and LG's panel technologies

OLED televisions come in three display panel types: WOLED, QD-OLED, and RGB Tandem OLED. WOLED is the most common display type that LG pioneered and continues to innovate on. These TVs use a white light source that passes through four filters to create color: red, green, blue, and white. The white subpixel layer helps brighten the image after it passes through the filters, but it comes at the cost of text clarity. This is the main technology you'll find in LG televisions and is ideal for high ambient-light environments.

Samsung shook up the OLED space in 2022 with QD-OLED. This technology uses a blue light source that passes through red and green quantum dots. Since the dots convert color rather than filtering it out, these panels tend to have a much wider color gamut and are significantly more energy efficient, which theoretically means they last longer. They're the gold standard for HDR displays, but quantum dot technology makes them ill-suited for bright living spaces; strong light hitting the panel can cause magenta glare.

RGB Tandem OLEDs use multiple emissive layers and a striped subpixel layout to boost brightness, reaching upwards of 1,000 nits per pixel on some television models. That said, the lack of quantum dot technology means RGB Tandems tend to have poorer color accuracy than Samsung's QD-OLEDs. RGB Tandem panels are worth a premium due to the high manufacturing cost.

Viewing experiences and controversies

On paper, Samsung's QD-OLED seems like the best option for most consumers. You can mitigate nearly all of the panel's weaknesses by minimizing light sources in your viewing space, and its color gamut is best-in-class for consumer televisions. However, the biggest deciding factor for OLED television has nothing to do with the television itself: it's the room you'll use it in. The best QD-OLED television will struggle in a room with high ambient light. And while LG does have some form of anti-glare on its OLED displays, it isn't enough to eliminate reflections entirely.

Software is also a major deciding factor. Samsung's amazing color saturation sadly can't be paired with Dolby Vision, as all Samsung OLED television models lack support for it — HDR10 is their substitute. Additionally, LG and Samsung televisions run different operating systems. LG's WebOS is supported for upwards of five years, while Samsung's latest Tizen OS will receive up to seven years of updates.

Brand trust shouldn't be disregarded here. Samsung is notorious for poor quality control across its products, including obscuring panel information in certain models. LG has had a more consistent track record, yet it has faced widespread criticism over privacy concerns. The company's terms of service allowed LG to record user conversations and sell them to advertisers. Consumer backlash led the company to release a statement soon after, though many haven't forgiven LG for the controversy.

Source: Engadget | Published: 2026-11-22 01:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.engadget.com/2310887/samsung-vs-lg-oled-tv-difference-between/

item.title: This is what can happen if too many devices are sharing your home network
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

This is what can happen if too many devices are sharing your home network

It doesn’t take much to bring a home network to its knees.

Any home network, regardless of efficiency and performance, can get overburdened when enough devices are connected, each vying for its own slice of the pie. When that happens, it's pretty obvious, with the infamous buffering circle plaguing screens, laggy online gaming, endless download times and the apocalypse landing on your doorstep. It doesn't take much to reach this point either. A single high-end smartphone can eat up quite a bit of bandwidth all by itself.

There are two potential limitations to consider. The first is the internet connection coming into your home via your Internet Service Provider (ISP). The second is the Wi-Fi connection between your router and your devices. A faster internet plan won't fix a weak signal from a router tucked into an out-of-the-way corner. On the flip side, a faster router can't do much with a slow internet service plan.

The knee-jerk reaction is to replace your router, upgrade your internet service plan speed and place the router in a more efficient position. That may indeed help, but not everyone can run out and purchase a Wi-Fi 6 or 7 router and hassle their ISP for faster service and an accordingly higher bill. But you shouldn't have to, as long as you don't mind playing with the numbers.

How many devices can your internet connection handle?

There's no reliable rule that says "100 Mbps internet connection supports a specific number of devices." Instead, estimate how many devices can run simultaneously without bogging everything else down. Netflix, for example, recommends a stable connection of at least 15 Mbps for each 4K stream. Three streams represent about 45 Mbps of recommended capacity without accounting for any overhead throughout the home (even coffee pots connect to Wi-Fi nowadays).

No, this doesn't mean each stream constantly consumes exactly 15 Mbps. We're just using it as a reference number for the purposes of planning things out. If there are 10 devices in the home, each using 10 Mbps, that would equal 100 Mbps. In that case, a 100 Mbps download speed (FCC's minimum broadband requirement) would leave no room to spare if all 10 devices are up and running at the same time. In reality, of course, speeds fluctuate, but it's a helpful little math drill to run if you're trying to stay organized and keep that ridiculous buffering circle off your TV screen.

Upload speeds are important for things like video calls or security cameras uploading footage of squirrels fighting in the front yard. Upload speeds are generally much slower than download speeds, thanks to asymmetrical broadband with ISPs allocating most of the bandwidth to downloads. Once you understand the speeds and the average consumption of a single device, you can plan large downloads or other Wi-Fi-intensive tasks for less busy times.

How many routers do I need in my home?

For the vast majority of households, one router is more than enough. A good mesh system or efficiently placed access points will solve most problems. An additional router makes sense in very specific situations. For instance, if your ISP has no choice but to run your wires and install your gateway in the far corner of your home, running an Ethernet cable from the gateway to a router in the center of your home might work out great.

But your best bet is to start with what you already have, and add to it incrementally on an "as-needed" basis. Switch stationary devices (PCs, consoles, TVs, etc.) to Ethernet, if possible, removing their traffic from Wi-Fi, although their internet activity will still share your broadband connection. A router upgrade is an option if you need something that can efficiently manage more devices. Just remember that advertised device capacity is great, but it can't overcome bandwidth limitations on your ISP plan.

If you opt for a mesh system to complement an ISP gateway, follow the setup instructions closely and don't leave both devices performing routing duties without checking the configuration. If the gateway and mesh remain in their default routing modes, it could create double NAT, which might cause an issue with online gaming or port forwarding. It doesn't need to get too complicated because the end point boils down to addressing what is constraining your system. Crunch the numbers first; decide which direction to go second. You got this!
